parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”), from ἀφορίζω (aphorízō, “I define, mark off or determine”), from ἀπό (apó, “off”) + ὁρίζω (horízō, “I divide, bound”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: the month of August (the eighth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Late Latin Agustus, from Latin augustus (“month of August”), from the agnomen Augustus (“venerable”) of Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus. Distantly related to the adjective augsts.

parole.significato: discussion, debate (conversation or debate, typically in public, where opposed opinions are presented and contrasted)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin discussiō, made into a fourth declension feminine noun.

parole.significato: inspiration (a sudden surge in mental activity that increases one's creative productivity; a sudden desire to create)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin inspīrātiō, from inspīrō (“to breathe into”), made into a 4th declension feminine noun ( + -ācija).
Ultimately from Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from Latin campus (“field”).

parole.significato: comfortable, convenient (where one feels at ease; having all comforts)
parole.testo: A borrowing, via other European languages (cf., e.g., French, English comfortable, German komfortabel, all with reflexes of the Latin suffix -abilis), ultimately from Late Latin confortō (“strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: modern (pertaining to the society, science, technique, art of a certain time period, usually the current one)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from Late Latin modernus, from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, “just now.”
Ultimately from Late Latin oppositiō, translating ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnō (“to set against”).
Ultimately from Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”).

parole.significato: psychology (the science of human behavior and the human mind)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: toxic, poisonous (having harmful effects on the organism)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin toxicus (“poisoned”), from Latin toxicum (“poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón) φάρμακον (phármakon, “poison for use on arrows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).

parole.significato: university, college (important institution of higher education, usually consisting of several faculties)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from Late Latin ūniversitās (“university”), accusative form ūniversitātem, adapted to Latvian patterns ( + -itāte).

Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
